## What you'll learn

- How to map each sample's reads to the gene catalog.
- How to keep only confident alignments, using alignment length and identity.
- How to count **inserts** per gene, and what to do with inserts that match several genes.
- How to judge how much of a community the catalog captures.

::: {.compact-diagram}
```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  R["Reads<br/>per sample"] --> A["Align to catalog<br/>bwa mem -a"]
  A --> F["Filter<br/>≥ 45 bp aligned<br/>≥ 95% identity"]
  F --> C["Count unique inserts<br/>per gene"]
  C --> T["Count table<br/>genes × samples"]
```
:::

## Map the reads

First index the catalog, then map each sample's reads. The forward (`.1`) and reverse (`.2`) reads are mapped **separately** and only paired up after filtering, so that a good alignment of one mate still counts when the other mate doesn't align.

```bash
mkdir -p alignments
bwa index catalog/catalog.fna

for s in metag1 metag2 metag3; do
  for r in 1 2; do
    bwa mem -a -t 4 catalog/catalog.fna data/reads/$s.$r.fq.gz \
      | samtools view -F 4 -b - > alignments/$s.r$r.bam
  done
done
```

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `bwa mem -a` | Report **all** alignments of a read, not just the best. Extra alignments are flagged as secondary. We need them to know when a read matches more than one gene. |
| `-t 4` | Number of threads |
| `samtools view -F 4` | Drop reads that didn't align (flag 4 = unmapped) |
| `-b` | Write BAM (compressed) output |

::: {.callout-note}
## Reads or inserts?
A read pair comes from one DNA fragment, the **insert**. We count inserts, not reads: if both mates of a pair hit a gene, that's one observation, not two. In the BAM files both mates share the same read name, which is how we pair them later.
:::

## Pull out what we need

For filtering we need, for each alignment, the read name, the SAM flag, the gene, the **CIGAR** string (how the read aligns) and the **NM** tag (number of mismatches and indels):

```bash
for s in metag1 metag2 metag3; do
  for r in 1 2; do
    samtools view alignments/$s.r$r.bam \
      | awk -v OFS='\t' '{ nm = "NA"; for (i = 12; i <= NF; i++) if ($i ~ /^NM:i:/) nm = substr($i, 6);
                           print $1, $2, $3, $6, nm }' \
      > alignments/$s.r$r.tsv
  done
done
head -6 alignments/metag1.r1.tsv
```

{{< include data/_excerpts/alignments.md >}}

Most reads align over their full length (`151M`: 151 matching positions). But look at `32M119S`: only 32 bases align, and the other 119 are **soft-clipped** (`S`), not part of the alignment. Is that read really from this gene?

## Filter: keep only confident alignments

We keep an alignment only if:

- at least **45 bases** are aligned, and
- the alignment is at least **95% identical**.

The aligned length comes from the CIGAR string: add up the matches (`M`), insertions (`I`) and deletions (`D`), and ignore clipped bases (`S`, `H`). Identity is the fraction of aligned positions that aren't edits: `(aligned length − NM) / aligned length`.

Let's work on a sample from metag1: all alignments of 3,000 inserts, from both mates.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_bw())
alignments <- read_csv("data/alignments_metag1_sample.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
alignments
```

### Exercise: aligned length from a CIGAR string

Complete the function so it returns the number of aligned positions in a CIGAR string. Test it: `"32M119S"` should give 32, and `"20M2I100M3D26M"` should give 151.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_cigar
aligned_length <- function(cigar) {
  # split "32M119S" into c("32M", "119S")
  ops <- regmatches(cigar, gregexpr("[0-9]+[MIDNSHP=X]", cigar))[[1]]
  n <- as.integer(sub("[A-Z=]$", "", ops))   # the numbers: 32, 119
  op <- sub("^[0-9]+", "", ops)               # the letters: "M", "S"
  sum(n[op %in% ______])
}

aligned_length("32M119S")
aligned_length("20M2I100M3D26M")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_cigar"}
Which operations are part of the alignment? Matches/mismatches `M`, insertions `I` and deletions `D` (`=` and `X` are the explicit forms of `M`). Write them as a character vector: `c("M", ...)`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_cigar"}
```r
aligned_length <- function(cigar) {
  ops <- regmatches(cigar, gregexpr("[0-9]+[MIDNSHP=X]", cigar))[[1]]
  n <- as.integer(sub("[A-Z=]$", "", ops))
  op <- sub("^[0-9]+", "", ops)
  sum(n[op %in% c("M", "I", "D", "=", "X")])
}

aligned_length("32M119S")
aligned_length("20M2I100M3D26M")
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_cigar
#| check: true
if (exists("aligned_length") &&
    aligned_length("32M119S") == 32 && aligned_length("20M2I100M3D26M") == 151 &&
    aligned_length("10S50M") == 50) {
  list(correct = TRUE, type = "success", message = "Correct: clipped bases are not counted, insertions and deletions are.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "error", message = "Not quite. Check: 32M119S → 32, 20M2I100M3D26M → 151, 10S50M → 50.")
}
```

Now apply it to every alignment and see how many pass:

```{webr}
aligned_length <- function(cigar) {
  ops <- regmatches(cigar, gregexpr("[0-9]+[MIDNSHP=X]", cigar))[[1]]
  n <- as.integer(sub("[A-Z=]$", "", ops))
  op <- sub("^[0-9]+", "", ops)
  sum(n[op %in% c("M", "I", "D", "=", "X")])
}

alignments <- alignments %>%
  mutate(aln_length = vapply(cigar, aligned_length, numeric(1)),
         identity = (aln_length - nm) / aln_length,
         passed = aln_length >= 45 & identity >= 0.95)

alignments %>% count(passed) %>% mutate(fraction = n / sum(n))

ggplot(alignments, aes(aln_length, identity, colour = passed)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.4, width = 0.5, height = 0.002) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 45, linetype = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "Aligned length (bp)", y = "Identity")
```

Most alignments are full-length and identical, which is expected: the catalog was built from these very samples. The alignments that fail are mostly **short**, where a read only partly overlaps a gene, for example at the gene's end.

## Count inserts per gene

After filtering, every insert has zero, one or more passing alignments, from either mate. An insert is **unique** if all its passing alignments hit **the same gene**.

```{webr}
inserts <- alignments %>%
  filter(passed) %>%
  group_by(insert) %>%
  summarise(n_genes = n_distinct(gene), gene = first(gene), .groups = "drop")

inserts %>% count(n_genes)
```

Most inserts hit one gene. Some hit two or more: **multi-mapping inserts**, typically from near-identical regions shared by different genes.

::: {.callout-note}
## What about multi-mapping inserts?
In this lesson we count **unique inserts only** and set multi-mapping ones aside. That's simple, but it undercounts genes that share sequence with others. A better approach distributes each multi-mapping insert among its genes **in proportion to how many unique inserts each gene has**. Our lab's tool **mCATs**, coming soon, does exactly this. We'll add a section on it here once it's public.
:::

### Exercise: count unique inserts per gene

Using `inserts`, keep the unique ones and count how many each gene gets. Which gene has the most?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_count
inserts %>%
  filter(______) %>%
  count(gene, sort = TRUE)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_count"}
Unique inserts are those with `n_genes == 1`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_count"}
```r
inserts %>%
  filter(n_genes == 1) %>%
  count(gene, sort = TRUE)
```
:::

## Run it for all samples

The workshop has a script with exactly these steps (filtering, pairing mates, unique counting) for every sample:

```bash
Rscript solutions/count_genes.R alignments data/reads counts
head counts/gene_counts.tsv
```

It writes `counts/gene_counts.tsv` (inserts per gene and sample) and `counts/mapping_stats.tsv`:

```{webr}
read_tsv("data/mapping_stats.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

The **mapping rate** is the fraction of all inserts that have at least one passing alignment. It tells you how much of the community your catalog represents.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {quiz} from "../../assets/quiz.ojs"

quiz("Here the mapping rate is above 96%. In a real study, mapping to a published catalog, you find 40%. What does that most likely mean?", [
  {text: "The sequencing failed", correct: false, why: "A sequencing problem would show up in quality control, not mainly as a low mapping rate."},
  {text: "Much of your community isn't in the catalog", correct: true, why: "Reads from organisms or genes missing from the catalog can't map. Our toy rate is so high because the catalog was built from these same three samples."},
  {text: "The filtering thresholds are too strict", correct: false, why: "45 bp and 95% identity remove only a few percent of alignments, as you saw above."}
])
```

## Check your work

```bash
./check c
```

## Key points

- Map forward and reverse reads separately with `bwa mem -a`, and pair them up after filtering.
- Keep alignments with **≥45 aligned bases** and **≥95% identity**, computed from the CIGAR string and NM tag.
- Count **inserts**, not reads. Here we count only unique inserts; proportional assignment of multi-mappers is coming with mCATs.
- The **mapping rate** tells you how much of the community the catalog captures.

The counts are raw: they still depend on gene length and sequencing depth. Part D shows how to normalise them, on a real dataset.
